title: Organic Molecules and Proteins
paras: Life is built from organic molecules—molecules based on carbon. Carbon atoms form stable bonds with each other and with hydrogen, oxygen, nitrogen, and other elements. They can make chains, rings, and branches of almost any length. No other element does this as readily under the conditions of a planet’s surface.

The simplest organic molecules are hydrocarbons, chains of carbon and hydrogen. Adding oxygen, nitrogen, or other atoms produces alcohols, acids, amines, and the rest of the vocabulary of organic chemistry. The same rules of bonding that govern a laboratory reaction govern the chemistry inside a cell. There is no separate vital chemistry. There is ordinary chemistry in a special setting.

Proteins are the workhorse molecules of life. They are chains of amino acids. Twenty amino acids are standard in the proteins of Earth life. The chain folds into a specific shape. The shape determines what the protein does. Some proteins are structural. Many are enzymes, catalysts that speed particular reactions by factors of millions or more. Without enzymes, the reactions of metabolism would be too slow to sustain life at ordinary temperatures.

The sequence of amino acids is specified by the gene. Change the gene, and in many cases you change the protein. The folding is determined by the sequence and by the cellular environment. Predicting the fold from the sequence was a long-standing problem. It is now largely solved for many proteins by computational methods trained on known structures. The experimental methods—X-ray crystallography and cryo-electron microscopy—still supply the reference structures.

Enzymes are specific. An enzyme that breaks down one sugar usually does not break down a different sugar. That specificity is why metabolism can be regulated. Pathways can be turned on or off by controlling the enzymes. Many drugs work by inhibiting a particular enzyme. The active site, the pocket where the reaction occurs, is the target.

Metabolism is the network of enzyme-catalyzed reactions that extract energy and build the molecules a cell needs. The central pathways—breaking down sugars, capturing energy in ATP, building amino acids and nucleotides—are shared across a wide range of life. The sharing is evidence of common ancestry. The variations are evidence of adaptation. A cell is a chemical system that maintains itself by running these pathways continuously, taking in fuel and exporting waste. Stop the flow, and the structure collapses.

title: The Cell
paras: The cell is the basic unit of life. Every organism is either a single cell or a collection of cells. The idea was established in the nineteenth century. It remains the foundation of biology.

Cells are of two broad kinds. Prokaryotic cells—bacteria and archaea—have no nucleus. Their DNA is in the cytoplasm. Eukaryotic cells—the cells of animals, plants, fungi, and protists—have a nucleus that holds the DNA, and they have other internal compartments. Mitochondria, which produce most of the cell’s usable energy, and chloroplasts, which carry out photosynthesis in plants and algae, were once free-living bacteria. They were taken in and became permanent. The evidence is their own DNA and the structure of their membranes.

A cell is bounded by a membrane made of lipids, with proteins embedded in it. The membrane controls what enters and leaves. Inside, the cytoplasm is crowded with molecules. It is not a bag of dilute solution. It is a dense, organized environment. In eukaryotic cells, an internal skeleton of protein filaments gives shape and moves cargo.

Cells reproduce by dividing. In prokaryotes the process is relatively simple. In eukaryotes, mitosis parcels the chromosomes so that each daughter cell receives a full set. Meiosis, used in sexual reproduction, halves the chromosome number so that fertilization restores it. Errors in these processes cause many genetic diseases and contribute to cancer.

The cell cycle is regulated. Checkpoints ensure that DNA is copied accurately and that the cell is ready to divide. Failures of regulation are a hallmark of cancer. Many cancer drugs target the machinery of division or the signals that drive it.

Cells communicate. They release signals, and they carry receptors that detect signals from other cells or from the environment. Development—the building of a body from a fertilized egg—is a conversation among cells, guided by genes that are turned on and off in sequence. The same genes appear in different animals, used in different combinations. A gene involved in building an eye in a fly has a relative involved in building an eye in a mouse. The parts were reused. The arrangements diverged.

Every cell alive today is the product of an unbroken sequence of divisions stretching back to the origin of life. The sequence is the deepest continuity in biology. Understanding the cell is understanding the unit in which that continuity is maintained.

title: The Circulation of the Blood and the Rise of Physiology
paras: For centuries the heart was thought to heat the blood and the blood was thought to move back and forth in the vessels. The lungs were thought to cool it. The idea came from the Greeks and was refined by Galen in the second century. It lasted more than a thousand years.

In 1628 William Harvey published a different account. He measured the volume of blood the heart pumps. The quantity was far too large for the blood to be made and consumed continuously. It had to circulate. He traced the path from the right side of the heart to the lungs, back to the left side, out to the body, and back again. The valves in the veins allow flow only toward the heart. The capillaries that complete the circuit were seen later, with the microscope.

Harvey’s method was quantitative. He counted and measured. The conclusion followed from the numbers. Physiology, the study of function, began to replace anatomy alone. The same approach was later applied to respiration, digestion, and the nervous system.

The blood carries oxygen, bound to hemoglobin, and nutrients. It carries waste. It carries hormones. The heart is a pump. The vessels are a closed system. The pressure is maintained by the heart and regulated by the vessels. High blood pressure damages the vessels and the organs they supply. Low pressure fails to deliver oxygen. The system is simple in outline and tightly regulated in practice.
The same quantitative habit that established circulation established the rest of modern physiology. Measure the input. Measure the output. Find the path. The method is still the one used today.

title: Spontaneous Generation and the Germ Theory
paras: For most of history it seemed obvious that life could arise from non-life. Maggots appeared in meat. Mice appeared in grain. The process was called spontaneous generation. It was accepted by Aristotle and by most writers after him.

Experiments gradually closed the claim. In the seventeenth century Francesco Redi showed that maggots did not appear in meat if flies were kept away. In the eighteenth century Lazzaro Spallanzani showed that broth, boiled and sealed, did not spoil. Critics said the sealing excluded a vital principle in the air. In the nineteenth century Louis Pasteur settled the question with flasks that had curved necks. Air could enter. Dust and microbes could not. The broth stayed clear. When the neck was broken, it spoiled. Life comes from life.

The same work opened the germ theory of disease. Specific diseases are caused by specific microorganisms. Robert Koch set the criteria: the organism must be found in the diseased host, grown in pure culture, produce the disease when introduced into a healthy host, and be recovered again. Those postulates identified the agents of anthrax, tuberculosis, cholera, and many others.

Vaccination uses the immune system’s memory. Edward Jenner showed that cowpox protected against smallpox. Pasteur developed weakened strains that protected against other diseases. Antibiotics, beginning with penicillin, kill or stop bacteria without killing the host. Viruses are not affected by antibiotics. They are stopped by the immune system, by vaccines, or by antiviral drugs.

The disproof of spontaneous generation did not close the question of how life began. It closed the claim that life arises readily and continuously under ordinary conditions. The origin of life is a separate problem, pushed back to the early Earth, where conditions were different and time was long.

title: Classification and the Tree of Life
paras: Aristotle listed hundreds of animals and grouped them. He noticed that the dolphin, though it looks like a fish and lives in the sea, breathes air and bears live young. He placed it with the mammals. The observation was correct. The principle was that structure and function matter more than habitat.

Carl Linnaeus, in the eighteenth century, gave the system its modern form. Every species receives a two-part name, genus and species. Species are grouped into genera, genera into families, families into orders, orders into classes, classes into phyla, phyla into kingdoms. The ranks are a filing system. They are useful for communication. They are not the deepest fact.

The deepest fact is descent. Darwin argued that the groups exist because of common ancestry. The tree of life is the diagram of that ancestry. Modern classification aims to make the groups reflect the branches of the tree. A group that includes an ancestor and all its descendants is monophyletic. Groups that do not are revised or abandoned.

The evidence is now molecular as well as anatomical. DNA sequences can be compared. The more similar the sequences, the more recent the common ancestor, in general. The comparisons have rearranged some branches. Birds are nested inside the dinosaurs. Fungi are closer to animals than to plants. The three domains—Bacteria, Archaea, and Eukarya—replace the older two-kingdom or five-kingdom schemes.

The number of described species is on the order of two million. The total number of species alive today is estimated in the millions more. Most are insects, microbes, and other small organisms. Extinction removes branches. Speciation adds them. The tree is not static. Classification is an attempt to describe it at a moment in time.

title: Genetics Before DNA
paras: Darwin’s theory of natural selection required that offspring resemble their parents and that variation exist. It did not explain how the resemblance or the variation was transmitted. The mechanism was missing.

Gregor Mendel, working with pea plants in the 1860s, supplied the beginning of the mechanism. Traits are controlled by factors that come in pairs. One factor can dominate the other. The factors separate when gametes are formed and recombine at fertilization. The ratios in the offspring follow from the combinations. Mendel’s work was ignored for decades and rediscovered around 1900.

The factors are genes. They are carried on chromosomes. Chromosomes are visible under the microscope. They duplicate and separate in mitosis so that each daughter cell receives a full set. In meiosis they pair and separate so that each gamete receives half the set. Fertilization restores the full number. The behavior of the chromosomes matches the behavior of Mendel’s factors.

Mutations are changes in genes. They arise spontaneously at low rates. Radiation and certain chemicals raise the rate. Most mutations are neutral or harmful. A few are beneficial in a given environment. Natural selection acts on the variation that mutation supplies. The combination of mutation, selection, and the Mendelian transmission of genes is the modern synthesis. It is the working account of evolution.

The physical nature of the gene was unknown until the middle of the twentieth century. Experiments showed that DNA, not protein, carries the genetic information. The structure of DNA, a double helix with complementary bases, explained how it can be copied. The genetic code maps triplets of bases to amino acids. The code is nearly universal. The universality is evidence of common ancestry.
The history from Mendel’s ratios to the structure of DNA took less than a century. The facts accumulated. The explanations followed. The same pattern continues.

title: Vitamins, Hormones, and the Chemical Control of the Body
paras: In the early twentieth century, diseases such as scurvy, beriberi, and rickets were traced to missing substances in the diet. The substances were named vitamins. They are required in small amounts. Some are cofactors for enzymes. Vitamin C is needed for the synthesis of collagen. The B vitamins are involved in energy metabolism. Vitamin D regulates calcium. Deficiency produces specific diseases. Excess of some vitamins also produces harm. The discovery converted nutrition from general advice about food into a chemistry of specific molecules.

Hormones are chemical signals produced by glands and carried in the blood. Insulin, from the pancreas, lowers blood sugar. Its absence or ineffectiveness produces diabetes. Thyroid hormone regulates metabolic rate. Adrenaline prepares the body for action. Sex hormones regulate reproduction. Growth hormone regulates growth. The endocrine system and the nervous system are the two main networks of control. They interact. Many signals are used by both.

Blood groups are determined by molecules on the surface of red cells. The ABO system and the Rh system are the best known. Transfusion requires matching. Mismatch can destroy the transfused cells. The groups are inherited in a Mendelian pattern. They are also useful as markers in genetics and in anthropology.

The chemical control of the body is precise. Concentrations are regulated by feedback. Too much of a hormone usually suppresses its own production. Too little stimulates it. The same logic appears in enzyme pathways and in gene regulation. The body is a set of chemical systems that maintain themselves by continuous adjustment. When the adjustment fails, disease follows. When the missing molecule can be supplied, as with insulin or a vitamin, the failure can often be corrected.

title: The Double Helix
paras: DNA is a double helix. Two strands of sugar and phosphate wind around each other. The bases point inward and pair. Adenine pairs with thymine. Guanine pairs with cytosine. The pairs are held by hydrogen bonds. The two strands run in opposite directions. The structure was proposed by James Watson and Francis Crick in 1953.

The proposal rested on several lines of evidence. Erwin Chargaff had shown that in any sample of DNA the amount of adenine equals the amount of thymine, and the amount of guanine equals the amount of cytosine. The equality suggested pairing. X-ray diffraction images of DNA fibers, produced by Rosalind Franklin and Raymond Gosling at King’s College London, and by Maurice Wilkins, showed that the molecule is helical and supplied its dimensions. The best-known image, Photograph 51, is an X-shaped pattern characteristic of a helix. The pitch is about 3.4 nanometers. There are about ten base pairs per turn. The diameter is about 2 nanometers.

Franklin’s data reached Watson and Crick indirectly. Wilkins showed Watson Photograph 51. A report summarizing Franklin’s measurements was also seen. Watson and Crick used the constraints to build a physical model. Earlier attempts had failed because the chemistry was wrong. The successful model placed the sugar-phosphate backbones on the outside and the base pairs on the inside. The pairing of A with T and G with C made every rung the same width. The strands are antiparallel. The structure immediately suggested a copying mechanism. Each strand can serve as a template for a new complementary strand. Watson and Crick noted the implication in their paper.

Three papers appeared together in *Nature* in April 1953. One by Watson and Crick presented the model. One by Wilkins and colleagues presented diffraction data. One by Franklin and Gosling presented their X-ray results. Watson, Crick, and Wilkins received the Nobel Prize in 1962. Franklin had died in 1958 and was not eligible.

The structure explains how genetic information is stored and copied. The sequence of bases is the information. The complementary pairing is the copying rule. Mutations are changes in the sequence. The same double helix is found in bacteria, plants, animals, and humans. The differences are in the sequence, not in the architecture. The architecture is what makes inheritance possible.

title: The Structure and Replication of DNA
paras: The 1953 paper by Watson and Crick proposed a specific structure for the salt of deoxyribose nucleic acid. Two helical chains coil around the same axis. The chains are related by a dyad perpendicular to the fiber axis, so the sequences of atoms run in opposite directions. The bases are on the inside. The phosphates are on the outside. There is a residue every 3.4 angstroms along the axis. The angle between adjacent residues is 36 degrees, so the structure repeats after 10 residues, or 34 angstroms. The distance of a phosphorus atom from the axis is about 10 angstroms.

The chains are held together by hydrogen-bonded pairs of bases. One member of each pair is a purine and the other is a pyrimidine. Adenine pairs with thymine. Guanine pairs with cytosine. The pairing accounts for Chargaff’s ratios. It also makes every rung the same width, so the backbone is regular. The structure is open and contains a good deal of water. At lower water content the bases tilt and the structure becomes more compact. That matches the observation of two forms, A and B, depending on humidity.

A second paper by Watson and Crick, published weeks later, spelled out the genetical implications. The two chains are complementary. The sequence on one determines the sequence on the other. Before duplication the hydrogen bonds break and the chains unwind and separate. Each chain then serves as a template for a new complementary chain. The result is two pairs where there was one. The sequence is duplicated exactly. The genetic information is carried in the sequence of the bases. The paper did not explain how that sequence specifies proteins. That explanation came later.

The X-ray papers published with the model supplied the supporting measurements. Franklin and Gosling described the B form as helical, with a pitch of about 34 angstroms, about ten nucleotides per turn, and a diameter of about 20 angstroms. The phosphate groups lie on the outside. Wilkins and colleagues reported similar dimensions from other samples and noted that the pattern is consistent with a helical structure. The model fit the data. Later crystallographic work confirmed the coordinates in detail.

The technical result is a molecule that can store a sequence and copy it. The sequence is the information. The complementary pairing is the copying rule. Everything that followed in molecular biology rests on that architecture.

title: Quantum Biology
paras: Most biological processes are well described by classical chemistry. A few involve quantum effects that cannot be ignored.

Enzyme catalysis sometimes uses tunneling. In hydrogen-transfer reactions the proton or hydrogen atom can pass through the energy barrier rather than over it. The rate is higher than a classical calculation predicts. Kinetic isotope effects—the change in rate when hydrogen is replaced by deuterium—are larger than expected from mass alone and are consistent with tunneling. The effect is temperature-dependent in ways that match quantum models.

Photosynthetic light-harvesting complexes transfer energy from antenna pigments to the reaction center with high efficiency. Spectroscopic measurements show coherent oscillations in the energy transfer. The coherence persists for hundreds of femtoseconds at physiological temperatures. Whether the coherence improves the efficiency under natural conditions or is a side effect of the structure is still under study. The observation is established. The functional importance is not fully settled.

Avian magnetoreception is another candidate. Some migratory birds orient using the Earth’s magnetic field. One proposed mechanism is a radical-pair reaction in cryptochrome proteins in the eye. The yield of the reaction depends on the orientation of the radical pair relative to the magnetic field because of the interplay of electron spins. The mechanism is plausible and consistent with behavioral experiments. Direct proof that it is the sensor used by the bird is still incomplete.

Quantum effects in biology are real where they have been measured. They do not require that the organism maintain macroscopic coherence. They occur in specific reactions where the energy barriers, the timescales, and the isolation from the environment allow them. The majority of cellular chemistry remains classical. The exceptions show that evolution can use quantum mechanics when it is available.

title: Endosymbiosis and Multicellularity
paras: Eukaryotic cells contain mitochondria. Plant cells also contain chloroplasts. Both organelles have their own DNA, their own ribosomes, and double membranes. The DNA is circular, like bacterial DNA. The sequences show that mitochondria are related to alphaproteobacteria and chloroplasts to cyanobacteria. The organelles were once free-living bacteria that became permanent residents of host cells. The process is endosymbiosis.

The host gained the ability to produce ATP by oxidative phosphorylation or to fix carbon by photosynthesis. The endosymbiont gained a stable environment and a supply of nutrients. Over time most of the endosymbiont’s genes were transferred to the host nucleus. The organelles retained a reduced genome that encodes some of their own proteins. The arrangement is stable. It occurred once for mitochondria, early in eukaryotic history, and once for the primary chloroplast, in the ancestor of the Archaeplastida. Secondary endosymbioses, in which a eukaryotic cell engulfed another eukaryote that already had a chloroplast, occurred several times and produced the chloroplasts of other algal groups.

Multicellularity evolved independently many times. Animals, plants, fungi, and several groups of algae and bacteria all contain multicellular species. The transition requires cells to adhere, to communicate, and to differentiate. In animals the extracellular matrix and cell-adhesion molecules hold cells together. Signaling pathways control division and specialization. Programmed cell death removes cells that are no longer needed. The genetic toolkit for these functions existed in unicellular ancestors and was co-opted. The Cambrian radiation, about 540 million years ago, produced most of the major animal body plans in a geologically short interval. The causes are debated. They include rising oxygen, ecological interactions, and the evolution of developmental gene networks. The fossil record shows the outcome. The precise triggers remain under study.

title: Natural Selection Without a Designer
paras: The appearance of design in living things is real. The eye focuses. The wing generates lift. The enzyme catalyzes a reaction at a rate that would otherwise take longer than the age of the universe. For centuries the inference was that such arrangements required a designer. The inference is unnecessary.

Natural selection is a process that produces cumulative adaptation without foresight. Variation exists. Some variants leave more offspring than others. The difference is heritable. Over generations the population changes. The change is not random. It is directed by the differential success of the variants in the environment they actually inhabit. The direction is local and retrospective. It does not aim at a distant goal. It does not require that any organism understand the process.

The cumulative character is essential. A single mutation rarely produces a complex organ. A sequence of mutations, each preserved because it conferred a small advantage in its own generation, can. The intermediates need not be useful for the final function. They need only be useful for something at the time they appear. The history is recoverable in the fossil record, in comparative anatomy, and in the sequences of genes. The same gene families appear in organisms that use them for different purposes. The pattern is the pattern of descent with modification, not the pattern of separate creation.

The process has no designer and no plan. It also has no guarantee of progress in any global sense. Lineages go extinct. Complexity can decrease. What it does guarantee is that, given variation, heritability, and differential reproduction, adaptation will accumulate where the conditions allow. The conditions have allowed it for more than three billion years. The result is the diversity of life. The mechanism is ordinary. The outcome is not.

title: Quantum Effects in Genetics
paras: Most genetic processes are classical. Base pairing, replication, transcription, and translation are described by ordinary chemistry. A few steps show quantum signatures that affect the outcome.

Proton tunneling contributes to some mutation rates. In DNA the hydrogen bonds that hold base pairs together can shift by tunneling. The tautomeric forms that result can mispair during replication. The rate is low. It is not zero. The contribution is measurable in some systems by comparing rates in ordinary water and in heavy water. The difference is consistent with a tunneling component. The bulk of mutations still arise from other causes: copying errors, chemical damage, and radiation. Tunneling is one channel among several.

Electron transfer in some repair enzymes and in photosynthetic reaction centers proceeds by tunneling. The distance dependence and the temperature dependence match quantum calculations. The proteins position the donors and acceptors so that the tunneling rate is useful. The positioning is the product of selection. The tunneling itself is a physical fact that selection has used.

No evidence currently supports the claim that genetic information is stored or processed in a macroscopic quantum superposition inside the cell. Decoherence times at biological temperatures and in the wet environment of the nucleus are extremely short. The successful descriptions of heredity, development, and evolution remain classical. The quantum contributions that have been demonstrated are local, specific, and already incorporated into the ordinary chemical account. They do not require a separate quantum genetics. They show that the chemistry of life includes the quantum mechanics of its atoms.

title: Adaptive Mutation and Quantum Coherence
paras: In 1999 Johnjoe McFadden and Jim Al-Khalili proposed a quantum model for adaptive mutation. Adaptive mutation is the reported phenomenon in which certain mutations appear more frequently when they confer an advantage than when they are neutral. The classical expectation is that mutation rates are independent of utility. The observations, first described in bacteria under starvation, have been disputed. Some are explained by ordinary growth and selection on pre-existing variants. Others remain unresolved.

The quantum proposal begins with proton tunneling in DNA base pairs. A proton can occupy either of two positions. The two positions correspond to different base-pairing possibilities. The model treats the proton as remaining in a coherent superposition of the two positions for a biologically relevant time. Interaction with an environment that contains a usable substrate is argued to accelerate decoherence and thereby increase the rate at which the mutant state is realized. The estimated decoherence time in the model is on the order of seconds. That is long enough, in principle, for the proposed effect.

The proposal has not been confirmed. Direct measurements of coherence in DNA under cellular conditions have not shown the required superposition. Decoherence calculations that include more of the molecular environment yield shorter times. The adaptive-mutation experiments themselves have alternative classical explanations in many cases. The idea remains a possible mechanism for a disputed phenomenon. It is not an established modification of evolutionary theory.

McFadden and Al-Khalili later surveyed a wider set of quantum effects in biology: tunneling in enzymes, coherent energy transfer in photosynthesis, the radical-pair mechanism for magnetoreception, and a proposed vibration-assisted tunneling in olfaction. Some of these effects are measured. Their functional importance varies. The adaptive-mutation model is the most specific claim that quantum coherence could bias the generation of heritable variation. That claim is still open. The broader observation that quantum mechanics is part of the chemistry of life is not.

title: Quantum Biology and Evolution
paras: Evolution is a classical process at the scale of populations. Mutation, selection, drift, and recombination are described by ordinary population genetics. The underlying chemistry of mutation and catalysis includes quantum steps. Those steps do not change the structure of the evolutionary account. They change the rates and the channels through which variation appears.

Proton and electron tunneling contribute to mutation. A proton that tunnels across a hydrogen bond in a base pair can produce a tautomeric form that mispairs. The contribution is small compared with copying errors and chemical damage. It is measurable in some systems by isotope effects. Electron tunneling occurs in the active sites of some repair enzymes. The proteins have evolved to position the reactants so that the tunneling rate is useful. The positioning is classical. The transfer step is quantum. Selection acts on the outcome, not on the mechanism.

Photosynthetic energy transfer and enzyme catalysis show coherent or tunneling contributions under physiological conditions. These processes affect the efficiency with which organisms capture energy and carry out metabolism. Efficiency is a selectable trait. Organisms that harness the quantum step more effectively leave more offspring, other things equal. The quantum step itself is not selected. The molecular architecture that makes the step available is selected. The distinction matters. Evolution does not need to “know” about quantum mechanics. It needs only to retain variants that work.

No established mechanism allows a cell to maintain a macroscopic superposition of genetic states and to collapse that superposition preferentially toward adaptive outcomes. The adaptive-mutation model remains a proposal. Decoherence in the cellular environment is rapid. The successful description of the origin and spread of adaptations continues to be the classical one: variation arises, most of it is neutral or deleterious, a fraction is advantageous, and selection increases the frequency of the advantageous fraction. Quantum mechanics is part of the physics that generates the variation and powers the metabolism. It is not a separate evolutionary force.

The practical consequence is modest and real. Calculations of mutation rates, of catalytic rates, and of energy-transfer efficiency are more accurate when the quantum channels are included. The evolutionary conclusions drawn from those rates do not change. The tree of life, the genetic code, and the history of adaptations remain the same. Quantum biology refines the chemistry. It does not rewrite the theory of evolution.

title: Cell Theory and Germ Theory
paras: The cell theory states that all living organisms are composed of cells and that cells arise only from pre-existing cells. The statement was assembled in the nineteenth century from observations by Schleiden, Schwann, and Virchow. It replaced earlier views that living matter could arise spontaneously or that tissues were continuous substances. Every organism examined since has confirmed the rule. Viruses are not cells, but they replicate only inside cells.

The germ theory states that many diseases are caused by microorganisms. Pasteur’s experiments on fermentation and putrefaction, and Koch’s isolation of specific pathogens, established the link. The same organisms that cause disease can be cultured, identified, and, in many cases, killed or blocked. Antisepsis, antibiotics, and vaccines followed. The theory does not claim that every illness is infectious. It claims that infectious illnesses have microbial causes that can be demonstrated.

Both theories are now foundational. Cell theory organizes development, physiology, and evolution. Germ theory organizes public health and medicine. Neither required a new force. Both followed from the consistent application of microscopy, staining, and controlled experiment. The results are independent of the particular wording in which they were first announced. The observations remain.

title: Mendel and the Chromosomes
paras: Gregor Mendel crossed pea plants that differed in clear traits and counted the offspring. Tall crossed with dwarf gave all tall in the first generation. Self-pollination of those hybrids gave three tall to one dwarf in the next. The dwarf trait had not disappeared. It had been hidden. Mendel proposed that each plant carries two factors for each trait, that the factors separate when gametes form, and that one factor can mask the other. The ratios followed. The same pattern held for other traits he tested.

The factors are now called genes. They are segments of DNA. The separation Mendel inferred is the separation of homologous chromosomes in meiosis. Each gamete receives one member of each pair. Fertilization restores the pair. The masking is dominance. The hidden factor is recessive. When both copies are recessive the trait appears. The arithmetic is the same whether the factors are abstract or molecular.

The work was published in 1866 and ignored. It was rediscovered in 1900 by investigators who had reached the same ratios. Within a few years the factors were located on chromosomes. Sutton and Boveri noted that chromosomes behave as Mendel’s factors must behave. Morgan’s group in fruit flies mapped genes to specific positions by measuring how often traits are inherited together. Linkage and recombination became measurable. The chromosome theory of inheritance was established.

The theory accounts for the transmission of traits. It does not by itself account for the origin of new traits. That required the later recognition of mutation. Together, Mendelian transmission and mutational variation supplied the genetic mechanism that Darwin’s theory had lacked. The mechanism is now molecular. The ratios Mendel counted remain.

title: Microbiology
paras: Microbiology is the study of organisms too small to see without magnification. The group includes bacteria, archaea, many fungi, protists, and viruses. Bacteria and archaea are prokaryotes. They lack a membrane-bound nucleus. Their DNA is a circular chromosome in the cytoplasm, often accompanied by smaller plasmids. Eukaryotic microbes have nuclei and organelles.

Bacteria reproduce by binary fission. Under favorable conditions some species double in twenty minutes. They exchange genes by transformation, transduction, and conjugation. These processes move DNA between cells that are not parent and offspring. The result is rapid spread of traits, including antibiotic resistance.

Archaea resemble bacteria in size and simplicity but differ in membrane lipids, cell-wall chemistry, and the machinery of transcription and translation. Many live in extremes of temperature, salinity, or acidity. Some produce methane. Their ribosomal RNA sequences place them on a separate branch of the tree of life.

Fungi and protists are eukaryotes. Yeasts are unicellular fungi used in fermentation. Molds form filaments. Protists include algae that photosynthesize and protozoa that ingest food. Amoebae are protists that move and feed by extending temporary projections of cytoplasm called pseudopods. The projections form by local changes in the cytoskeleton. The cell crawls toward food or away from harm. Some amoebae are free-living in soil and water. Others are parasitic.

Microbes drive the major chemical cycles of the planet. They fix nitrogen, produce oxygen, decompose organic matter, and generate methane. They also cause disease. The same tools—culture, microscopy, staining, and sequencing—identify both the beneficial and the pathogenic species. The distinction is ecological, not taxonomic.

title: Viruses
paras: Viruses are particles that replicate only inside living cells. They consist of nucleic acid enclosed in a protein coat. Some have a lipid envelope derived from the host membrane. The nucleic acid is DNA or RNA, single- or double-stranded, linear or circular. The coat protects the genome and, in many cases, attaches to a receptor on the host cell.

Outside a cell a virus is inert. It has no metabolism and no independent replication. Inside a susceptible cell it redirects the host machinery to copy its genome and synthesize its proteins. New particles assemble and leave, often destroying the cell. The host range is limited by the receptors the virus can bind. A virus that infects one species may be unable to infect another.

Bacteriophages infect bacteria. They were used to show that DNA, not protein, carries genetic information. Animal and plant viruses cause many diseases. Some insert their genome into the host chromosome and remain latent. Others kill the cell quickly. Retroviruses reverse-transcribe RNA into DNA that integrates into the host genome. The integrated form can be transmitted to daughter cells.

Viruses evolve. Mutation rates are high, especially in RNA viruses. Recombination and reassortment occur when multiple viruses infect the same cell. The result is rapid change in surface proteins and in host range. Vaccines and antiviral drugs select for resistant variants. The same processes that generate diversity in cellular organisms operate, at higher speed, in viruses.

Viruses are not classified as living by most definitions because they lack independent metabolism. They are biological entities that evolve and that affect every domain of life. They move genes between hosts, regulate microbial populations, and shape the evolution of immune systems. Their study is part of microbiology whether or not they are counted as organisms.

title: Amoebae
paras: Amoebae are unicellular eukaryotes that move by pseudopods. The pseudopod is a temporary extension of the cytoplasm. Actin filaments polymerize at the leading edge and push the membrane forward. Myosin and other motors contract at the rear. The cell advances. The same machinery is used for phagocytosis. The amoeba surrounds a particle of food, encloses it in a vesicle, and digests it with enzymes delivered from lysosomes.

Most amoebae are free-living. They inhabit soil, fresh water, and marine sediments. They feed on bacteria, algae, and detritus. A few species are parasitic. Entamoeba histolytica infects the human intestine and can invade the liver. Naegleria fowleri is free-living in warm water and can infect the brain if it enters through the nose. These cases are rare. Most amoebae never encounter a human host.

Amoebae were among the first microbes observed. Leeuwenhoek described them in the seventeenth century. Later workers used them to study cell movement, phagocytosis, and cytoplasmic streaming. The mechanisms proved to be general. The same actin–myosin system operates in the white blood cells of animals and in the crawling of many other cells. The amoeba is a convenient model because the entire organism is one cell and the behavior is visible under a light microscope.

The group is not a single evolutionary lineage. “Amoeba” describes a body plan that has evolved more than once. Some amoeboid organisms are closely related to animals and fungi. Others belong to distant branches of the eukaryotic tree. The shared appearance is convergent. The underlying cell biology is ancient.

title: Modern DNA Methods
paras: Restriction enzymes cut DNA at specific sequences. DNA ligase joins the ends. The combination allowed recombinant DNA in the 1970s. A gene from one organism could be inserted into a plasmid and propagated in bacteria. The technique produced insulin, growth hormone, and many other proteins.

The polymerase chain reaction amplifies a chosen segment of DNA exponentially. A pair of primers, a heat-stable polymerase, and thermal cycling generate millions of copies from a few molecules. Sequencing reads the order of bases. Sanger sequencing used chain-terminating nucleotides. Next-generation methods read millions of fragments in parallel. A human genome that once required years and hundreds of millions of dollars can now be sequenced in hours for hundreds of dollars.

CRISPR-Cas systems are adaptive immune mechanisms in bacteria. A guide RNA directs the Cas nuclease to a matching DNA sequence. The nuclease cuts. The cell repairs the break. Repair can disable the gene or, if a template is supplied, insert a new sequence. Base editors and prime editors change single bases or short stretches without double-strand breaks. The tools work in bacteria, plants, animals, and human cells. They are used in research, in agriculture, and in clinical trials for genetic disease.

Gene drives bias inheritance so that a chosen allele spreads through a population faster than Mendelian ratios allow. They have been demonstrated in insects in the laboratory. Their use outside containment is contested because the spread is designed to be difficult to reverse.

The methods are precise relative to earlier mutagenesis. They are not perfectly precise. Off-target cuts occur. Delivery to the right cells in a living organism remains difficult. The capability to read, write, and edit DNA at scale now exists. The limits are technical, regulatory, and ethical.

title: Cloning
paras: Cloning produces a genetic copy of an organism. In plants it is routine. Cuttings and tissue culture generate identical individuals. In animals the method is somatic-cell nuclear transfer. The nucleus of a somatic cell is placed in an enucleated egg. The reconstructed egg is stimulated to develop. The resulting animal has the nuclear genome of the donor.

Dolly the sheep was the first mammal cloned from an adult somatic cell. She was born in 1996. The success rate was low. Many reconstructed embryos failed. Those that developed sometimes showed abnormalities. Subsequent work produced cloned cattle, pigs, goats, cats, dogs, and other species. Efficiency has improved but remains far below natural reproduction.

In 2018 Chinese researchers produced the first cloned primates, two macaques, from fetal fibroblasts. A later rhesus monkey was cloned from fetal cells and required a non-cloned placenta. No healthy primate has been produced from an adult somatic cell. The reprogramming of an adult nucleus is incomplete in primates under current methods.

Reproductive cloning of humans has not been achieved. No verified human clone has been born. Therapeutic cloning, the production of embryonic stem cells genetically matched to a patient, has been performed in the laboratory. The embryos are not implanted. Most countries prohibit reproductive human cloning. A smaller number permit research on cloned human embryos under license. The technical barrier in primates remains high. The regulatory barrier is explicit.

title: Human Genetics
paras: The human genome contains about three billion base pairs and roughly twenty thousand protein-coding genes. Most of the sequence does not code for protein. Regulatory elements, introns, and repetitive DNA make up the majority. Variation among individuals is about one difference per thousand bases. Most variants are neutral. A minority affect traits or disease risk.

Monogenic disorders are caused by variants in a single gene. Sickle-cell disease, cystic fibrosis, and Huntington’s disease are examples. The inheritance follows Mendelian ratios when the variant is fully penetrant. Many common diseases are polygenic. Height, blood pressure, and susceptibility to type 2 diabetes or schizophrenia are influenced by thousands of variants of small effect, plus environment. Polygenic scores sum the effects. They are predictive in populations similar to the ones in which they were derived and less predictive in others.

Genome-wide association studies scan hundreds of thousands of people for statistical links between variants and traits. The links identify regions. They do not by themselves prove causation. Functional studies are required. The same methods have mapped genes that affect drug response, a field called pharmacogenetics. A variant that is harmless in one context can determine whether a drug is effective or toxic.

Editing the human germline changes DNA that can be inherited. In 2018 He Jiankui announced the birth of twins whose embryos had been edited at the CCR5 locus. The work was widely condemned. He was convicted in China of illegal medical practice and imprisoned. Chinese regulations now prohibit clinical research that alters germ cells or embryos for reproduction. Somatic editing, which affects only the treated individual, is in clinical trials for several diseases. The distinction between somatic and germline alteration is the current regulatory boundary.

title: The Human Body
paras: The body is a system of organs that maintain conditions compatible with the life of its cells. Temperature, acidity, salt balance, and the supply of oxygen and fuel are held within narrow ranges. The holding is called homeostasis. It is active. It costs energy. When it fails, illness follows.

Food supplies the energy and the building materials. Carbohydrates, fats, and proteins are broken down by digestion into sugars, fatty acids, and amino acids, which are absorbed and distributed. Vitamins and minerals are required in smaller amounts. Some, like vitamin C and the B vitamins, are cofactors for enzymes. Deficiency diseases—scurvy, rickets, beriberi—were traced to missing vitamins in the early twentieth century. The tracing was one of the clearest demonstrations that specific molecules have specific roles in the body.

Oxygen is carried by hemoglobin in red blood cells. The same protein that makes blood red binds oxygen in the lungs and releases it in the tissues. Carbon dioxide is carried back, mostly dissolved. The heart pumps the blood. The lungs exchange the gases. The system is simple in outline and finely regulated in practice. Exercise, altitude, and disease all change the demands. The body adjusts the rate of breathing and the output of the heart to match.

Hormones are chemical signals carried in the blood. Insulin, produced by the pancreas, regulates blood sugar. Thyroid hormone regulates metabolic rate. Sex hormones regulate reproduction and secondary characteristics. Growth hormone and others regulate growth and repair. The endocrine system and the nervous system are the two main communication networks. They overlap. Many signals are used by both.

The immune system distinguishes self from non-self and attacks the latter. It has an innate arm that responds quickly and broadly, and an adaptive arm that learns specific pathogens and remembers them. Vaccination is the deliberate use of that memory. Antibodies, produced by B cells, bind to specific targets. T cells kill infected cells or help coordinate the response. Autoimmune diseases occur when the distinction fails and the system attacks the body’s own tissues. Allergies occur when it overreacts to a harmless substance.

Aging, infection, injury, and genetic error are the main ways the system fails. Medicine is the attempt to restore or replace the failed function. Surgery, drugs, hormones, and, increasingly, cells and genes are the tools. The body is not a machine in the simple sense. It is a living system that repairs itself until it cannot. Understanding the repair, and its limits, is the practical face of physiology.

title: The Nervous System and the Brain
paras: The nervous system coordinates the body. It receives signals from the senses and from the internal organs. It sends signals to muscles and glands. It stores information and generates behavior.

The basic unit is the neuron. A neuron has a cell body, dendrites that receive signals, and an axon that carries signals away. The signal is an electrical impulse, the action potential. It is produced by the flow of ions across the membrane. Sodium and potassium are the main ions. The membrane is polarized at rest. When stimulated past a threshold, it depolarizes and the impulse travels. At the end of the axon the signal is usually passed to the next cell by a chemical neurotransmitter. Acetylcholine and many others are used. The synapse is the junction. Most drugs that affect the brain act at synapses.

The brain and spinal cord form the central nervous system. The peripheral nerves connect them to the rest of the body. The autonomic system controls involuntary functions—heart rate, digestion, pupil size—and has sympathetic and parasympathetic divisions that often oppose each other.

The brain has major divisions. The brainstem controls basic life functions: breathing, heart rate, arousal. The cerebellum coordinates movement and balance. The cerebrum is the largest part in humans. Its cortex is folded. The folds increase surface area. The cortex is divided into lobes. The frontal lobes are involved in planning, decision, and voluntary movement. The parietal lobes process touch and spatial information. The temporal lobes process hearing and aspects of memory. The occipital lobes process vision. The functions are specialized but interconnected. Damage to a region produces characteristic deficits.

The senses convert physical stimuli into nerve signals. The eye focuses light on the retina. Photoreceptors respond to light. The signals travel through the optic nerve to the brain. Color vision depends on three types of cones with different sensitivities. The ear converts sound waves into mechanical vibration and then into nerve signals in the cochlea. Balance is sensed by the vestibular organs in the inner ear. Taste and smell are chemical senses. Touch, temperature, and pain are sensed by receptors in the skin and elsewhere.

Reflexes are rapid, automatic responses. The knee-jerk reflex involves a sensory neuron, a motor neuron, and a synapse in the spinal cord. More complex behaviors involve the brain. Learning changes the strength of connections between neurons. Memory involves changes in synapses and, for long-term memory, changes in gene expression and structure.

Hormones interact with the nervous system. The hypothalamus links the two. It controls the pituitary, which controls other glands. Stress, growth, reproduction, and metabolism are regulated by both nerves and hormones. The brain is not separate from the body. It is the organ that integrates the signals and produces coordinated action. Its capacities—language, abstract thought, planning—are large. They are the product of the same cellular machinery that operates in every other tissue, arranged in a particular architecture.

title: The Structure of the Earth
paras: The Earth is not a uniform ball. It has layers, and the layers were inferred before they were directly sampled.

The outermost layer is the crust, thin and rigid. Under the oceans it is typically 5 to 10 kilometers thick. Under the continents it is thicker, often 30 to 50 kilometers. Below the crust is the mantle, a thick layer of hot rock that extends to about 2,900 kilometers depth. The mantle is solid but, over long times, flows slowly. At the center is the core, divided into a liquid outer core and a solid inner core, both made mostly of iron with some nickel and lighter elements. The inner core is solid because the pressure is high enough to keep iron solid despite the temperature.

The evidence for these layers came first from earthquake waves. P-waves and S-waves travel at different speeds and behave differently at boundaries. S-waves do not travel through liquid. Their absence in certain paths showed that the outer core is liquid. The speeds and reflections mapped the boundaries. Later, the composition was constrained by the density required to match the Earth’s total mass and by the chemistry of meteorites, which sample the material from which the planet formed.

The crust is not fixed. It is broken into plates that move. The idea of continental drift was proposed in detail by Alfred Wegener in 1912. He noted the fit of the continents, the match of fossils and rock formations across oceans, and evidence of past climates. The mechanism was missing, and the idea was resisted. In the 1960s, seafloor spreading and plate tectonics supplied the mechanism. New crust forms at mid-ocean ridges. Old crust sinks at trenches. Continents are carried with the plates. The Atlantic is widening. The Pacific is shrinking in places. Earthquakes and volcanoes concentrate at the boundaries.

The Earth’s magnetic field is generated by motion in the liquid outer core. The field reverses at irregular intervals. Those reversals are recorded in the seafloor as it forms, providing a tape of the spreading. The field also shields the surface from much of the solar wind. Without it, the atmosphere would be more vulnerable to stripping.

The age of the Earth is about 4.54 billion years, measured from the oldest meteorites and from the oldest terrestrial minerals. The oldest known crustal rocks are younger, because the surface has been recycled. Zircon crystals from Australia are more than 4.3 billion years old and show that continental crust and liquid water existed early.

Heat inside the Earth comes from leftover heat of formation and from radioactive decay. That heat drives the mantle’s slow convection, which drives the plates, and it supplies the energy for volcanoes and for the magnetic field. The surface we live on is the cool, thin skin of a planet that is still geologically active.

title: The Arrow of Time
paras: The laws of mechanics are nearly symmetric under the reversal of time. If a set of particle trajectories is allowed, the reversed trajectories are also allowed. A film of two billiard balls colliding looks almost the same run backward. The exception is friction and other dissipative processes, which convert organized motion into heat.

Thermodynamics supplies the direction. The second law states that the entropy of an isolated system does not decrease. Entropy is a measure of the number of microscopic arrangements consistent with the macroscopic state. A gas that fills a room has far more arrangements than the same gas confined to one corner. The probability of the gas spontaneously returning to the corner is negligible. The direction of time in everyday experience is the direction of increasing entropy.

The universe began in a state of low entropy. The hot, dense early universe was smooth. Gravity later clumped matter into stars and galaxies, increasing the entropy. The low-entropy initial condition is what allows the second law to define a direction. Without it, there would be no preferred direction for the growth of entropy. Why the initial condition was low-entropy is an open question. It is not explained by the second law itself.

Memory and records point in the same direction. A memory is a correlation between a present state and a past state. The formation of that correlation increases the entropy of the surroundings. We remember the past and not the future because the past is the direction of lower entropy. The same asymmetry appears in the fact that causes precede effects in ordinary experience. The microscopic laws do not enforce the asymmetry. The boundary condition does.

The arrow is not absolute in every sense. In small systems fluctuations can temporarily decrease entropy. The decreases are rare and short-lived. On the scales of everyday objects and of the universe as a whole, the second law holds. The direction of time that we experience is the direction in which entropy increases. That is the content of the thermodynamic arrow. Other arrows—the psychological arrow, the causal arrow—align with it under the low-entropy initial condition. The alignment is observed. The ultimate reason for the initial condition is not yet known.

title: Time Reversal
paras: The fundamental equations of classical mechanics, electromagnetism, and quantum mechanics are invariant under reversal of the time coordinate. If a sequence of events is allowed, the time-reversed sequence is also a solution. The equations do not prefer one direction.

The observed universe does. Entropy increases. Heat flows from hot to cold. Memory records the past, not the future. The asymmetry is statistical. A system that begins in a low-entropy state is overwhelmingly likely to evolve toward higher entropy. The early universe was in such a state. The microwave background and the smoothness of the large-scale geometry record that fact. Why the initial entropy was low is not explained by the time-symmetric equations.

Weak interactions violate time-reversal symmetry by a small amount. The violation has been measured in the decays of neutral kaons and B mesons. It is required by the observed excess of matter over antimatter. The effect is tiny. It does not account for the thermodynamic arrow. The thermodynamic arrow is explained by the initial condition, not by a fundamental asymmetry in the microscopic laws.

Time reversal is therefore a symmetry of the equations and a broken symmetry of the solutions we inhabit. The equations permit both directions. The universe we observe has a past boundary of low entropy and a future of higher entropy. The origin of that boundary remains an open question in cosmology.

title: Entropy
paras: Entropy is a measure of the number of microscopic arrangements that correspond to a given macroscopic state. A system with many accessible microstates has high entropy. A system with few has low entropy. The second law of thermodynamics states that the entropy of an isolated system does not decrease. It stays the same in reversible processes and increases in irreversible ones.

The law is statistical. Every microstate is equally likely. There are vastly more microstates that look disordered than microstates that look ordered. A system that begins in a low-entropy state is therefore overwhelmingly likely to evolve toward higher entropy. The reverse evolution is not forbidden. It is improbable to a degree that makes it unobservable in ordinary systems.

Heat flows from hot to cold because the combined system has more microstates when the temperatures are equal. Gases expand to fill their containers because the expanded state has more arrangements. Living organisms maintain low internal entropy by exporting entropy to their surroundings. The total entropy of organism plus surroundings still rises. The Sun’s increase in entropy supplies the margin that allows the decrease on Earth.

The early universe was in a state of remarkably low entropy. The microwave background is smooth to one part in a hundred thousand. That smoothness is a low-entropy condition for the gravitational field. The subsequent increase in entropy includes the formation of stars, galaxies, and black holes. Black holes have entropy proportional to the area of their event horizons. They dominate the entropy budget of the observable universe.

Entropy defines a direction in time. The microscopic equations are time-symmetric. The boundary condition of low entropy in the past is not. The second law is the macroscopic consequence of that boundary condition. Why the boundary condition was low remains unexplained.

title: The Direction of Time
paras: The microscopic laws of physics are invariant under time reversal. If a process is allowed, the time-reversed process is also a solution of the equations. Classical mechanics, electromagnetism, and the Schrödinger equation share this symmetry. The weak interaction violates it by a small, measured amount. The violation is insufficient to produce the observed arrow.

The thermodynamic arrow points from low entropy to high entropy. The early universe was gravitationally smooth and thermally uniform. That state has low entropy. Subsequent evolution increases entropy through the formation of structure, the burning of stars, and the growth of black holes. Memory, causation, and the psychological sense of passage align with this gradient. Records exist of the past because the past was the low-entropy boundary.

No fundamental law forbids the opposite gradient. A universe that began in a high-entropy state would not develop a consistent arrow. The existence of the arrow is therefore a fact about the boundary condition, not about the dynamical laws. Why the boundary condition was low-entropy remains an open question in cosmology. Proposals include special initial conditions, inflationary smoothing, and selection effects. None is established.

title: The Arrow of Time in Cosmology
paras: The thermodynamic arrow points from the low-entropy early universe to the higher-entropy present. The low entropy is not a consequence of the dynamical laws. It is a boundary condition. The microwave background is smooth. That smoothness is a low-entropy state for the gravitational field. Subsequent clumping into stars and black holes increases the entropy.

The psychological arrow—the fact that we remember the past and not the future—aligns with the thermodynamic arrow. Records form only when entropy increases. The cosmological arrow—the expansion itself—does not by itself define a direction. A contracting universe with the same low-entropy boundary condition would still have a thermodynamic arrow pointing away from that boundary.

Why the initial entropy was low remains unexplained. Proposals include special initial conditions, inflationary smoothing, and selection effects within a larger ensemble. None is established. The existence of the arrow is nevertheless an observed fact about the solution we inhabit.

title: Further Aspects of the Arrow of Time in Cosmology
paras: The thermodynamic arrow is aligned with the expansion. Entropy increases as the universe expands from a smooth, low-entropy initial state. The alignment is not automatic. A contracting universe with the same low-entropy boundary condition would have an arrow pointing away from that boundary, not toward it. The observed arrow therefore reflects the special initial condition, not the expansion itself.

Inflationary models push the low-entropy condition to still earlier times. They do not explain why the condition was satisfied. The explanation, if it exists, lies in quantum gravity or in a selection principle among possible initial states. No such principle is established. The arrow remains a boundary condition of the solution we inhabit.

title: Black Holes and Their Thermodynamics
paras: A black hole is a region of spacetime from which no signal can reach distant observers. The boundary is the event horizon. It is not a material surface. It is the set of points beyond which all future-directed paths remain inside. For a non-rotating black hole the radius of the horizon is the Schwarzschild radius, \( R_s = 2GM/c^2 \). For the Sun that radius is about three kilometers. For the Earth it is about nine millimeters. Nothing of ordinary density is compressed that far. Stellar cores that exceed the maximum mass for a neutron star can collapse past that point.

Once an object crosses the horizon, the geometry prevents escape. Tidal forces become extreme near a small black hole. They stretch an object along the radial direction and compress it transversely. For a supermassive black hole the horizon is so large that the tidal forces at the horizon itself are mild. The singularity, where curvature becomes infinite according to classical general relativity, lies in the future of any observer who crosses the horizon.

Black holes have thermodynamic properties. The area of the event horizon never decreases in classical processes. That behavior is analogous to the second law of thermodynamics. Bekenstein proposed that the entropy of a black hole is proportional to the area of its horizon. Hawking showed that a black hole emits thermal radiation at a temperature inversely proportional to its mass. The temperature for a solar-mass black hole is about \( 6 \times 10^{-8} \) K, far below the temperature of the cosmic microwave background. Smaller black holes are hotter and evaporate faster. The entropy is \( S = A/4 \) in Planck units. Information about what fell in is encoded on the horizon, not in the volume. That result is one of the motivations for holographic ideas in quantum gravity.

The classical theory predicts a singularity. Quantum effects are expected to become important near the singularity and possibly near the horizon. No complete theory of quantum gravity yet exists that describes the interior. The exterior geometry, the horizon, the radiation, and the area law are established within the combined framework of general relativity and quantum field theory in curved spacetime. Observations of gravitational waves from merging black holes, of the orbits of stars around the galactic center, and of the shadow of the black hole in M87 match the predictions of the classical theory outside the horizon.

title: Black Holes in Astrophysics
paras: A black hole is a region from which no signal can escape to infinity. The boundary is the event horizon. For a non-rotating hole the horizon radius is \( 2GM/c^2 \). Stellar-mass black holes form in the collapse of massive stars. Supermassive black holes, millions to billions of solar masses, occupy the centres of most large galaxies.

The Event Horizon Telescope has imaged the shadow of the black hole in M87 and of the black hole at the centre of the Milky Way. The diameter of the shadow matches the prediction of general relativity. Gravitational-wave detectors have recorded the mergers of stellar-mass black holes. The waveforms match the numerical solutions of the Einstein equation.

Matter falling toward a black hole forms an accretion disk. Viscosity transports angular momentum outward and allows the gas to spiral inward. The released gravitational energy heats the disk and can power quasars and X-ray binaries. The efficiency of conversion of rest mass to radiation can exceed 10 percent, higher than nuclear fusion.

No information about the interior can reach an external observer. The classical theory ends at the singularity. Quantum effects are expected to modify the singularity, but no complete theory yet exists. The exterior geometry is nevertheless accurately described by the Kerr or Schwarzschild solution.

title: The Information Paradox
paras: Hawking radiation is thermal. A black hole that forms from a pure quantum state and evaporates completely therefore appears to leave a mixed state. The evolution from pure to mixed violates unitarity. That is the information paradox.

Several resolutions have been proposed. The information may be returned in subtle correlations in the radiation. It may be stored in a remnant. It may be lost. The AdS/CFT correspondence indicates that the evolution is unitary in at least some cases. The correspondence does not yet supply an explicit mechanism that works for an evaporating black hole in asymptotically flat space.

Recent calculations of the entropy of the radiation suggest that the Page curve is reproduced once quantum extremal surfaces are included. The entropy of the radiation rises and then falls, consistent with unitarity. The calculations are still limited to simplified models. They indicate that information is not lost, but they do not yet describe the detailed recovery process for a realistic black hole.
The paradox remains a sharp statement of the tension between general relativity and quantum mechanics. Its resolution will require a theory that handles both.

title: Black Holes
paras: A black hole is a region of spacetime from which no signal can reach distant observers. The boundary of the region is the event horizon. In the Schwarzschild solution the horizon lies at the radius \( r_s = 2GM/c^2 \). For a solar-mass object the radius is 3 km. Inside the horizon every future-directed path ends at the central singularity.

Astrophysical black holes form by the collapse of massive stellar cores and by the subsequent growth of those seeds through accretion and mergers. Stellar-mass black holes are observed as X-ray binaries and as the sources of gravitational-wave signals. Supermassive black holes, millions to billions of solar masses, occupy the centres of most large galaxies. The Event Horizon Telescope has imaged the shadows of the black holes in M87 and in the Milky Way; the measured diameters match the general-relativistic prediction.

Matter falling toward a black hole forms an accretion disk. Viscous transport of angular momentum allows the gas to spiral inward, converting gravitational potential energy into heat and radiation. The efficiency can exceed 10 percent of the rest mass for a rapidly rotating hole—higher than nuclear fusion. The same disks power quasars and many galactic X-ray sources.

The classical theory predicts that the horizon area never decreases and that the surface gravity is constant over the horizon. When quantum field theory is included, the horizon emits thermal radiation at the Hawking temperature \( \hbar c^3/(8\pi GMk_B) \). The radiation carries the Bekenstein–Hawking entropy \( k_Bc^3A/(4G\hbar) \). Complete evaporation of an initially pure state appears to produce a mixed state, raising the information paradox. Recent calculations in simplified models suggest that unitarity is preserved, but no consensus mechanism yet exists for realistic black holes.
No observation contradicts the general-relativistic description of the exterior. The interior, the singularity, and the ultimate fate of the information remain outside present experimental reach.

title: The Black-Hole Information Paradox
paras: Hawking radiation is thermal. A black hole that forms from a pure quantum state and evaporates completely therefore appears to leave behind a mixed state of radiation. The map from pure to mixed states is non-unitary. Unitarity is a fundamental requirement of quantum mechanics. The conflict is the information paradox.

The paradox becomes acute for an old black hole. Once more than half the initial entropy has been radiated, the remaining black hole has less entropy than the radiation already emitted. If the evaporation continues to be thermal, the total state cannot purify. The Page curve—the entanglement entropy of the radiation—must therefore rise and then fall if unitarity is to be preserved. A purely thermal spectrum produces a curve that rises indefinitely.

Recent calculations that include quantum extremal surfaces reproduce a Page curve that turns over. The island formula assigns part of the black-hole interior to the entanglement wedge of the radiation after the Page time. The result suggests that information is released in subtle correlations and that the final state is pure. The calculations have been performed in simplified models and in low-dimensional gravity. Their extension to realistic, asymptotically flat black holes is incomplete.

Alternative proposals include remnants that store the information, modifications of the radiation at late times, and non-unitary evolution. None is free of difficulties. The island calculations are the first to recover the Page curve from a semi-classical gravitational path integral. They indicate that the paradox may be resolved without abandoning unitarity or introducing new degrees of freedom beyond those already present in quantum gravity. A fully controlled demonstration for an evaporating four-dimensional black hole does not yet exist.

title: Hawking Radiation
paras: Hawking radiation is the thermal flux emitted by a black hole. It arises when quantum fields propagate on the curved spacetime of a collapsing body. Modes that straddle the horizon become entangled. The exterior member of each pair escapes to infinity as a real particle. The spectrum seen by a distant observer is thermal at the temperature
\[ T = \frac{\hbar c^3}{8\pi G M k_B}. \]

The temperature is inversely proportional to the mass. A solar-mass hole radiates at about \( 10^{-7} \) K, far below the cosmic microwave background. A hole of mass \( 10^{12} \) kg radiates at room temperature and evaporates on a timescale comparable to the age of the universe. The power scales as \( 1/M^2 \). Evaporation therefore accelerates as the hole shrinks.

The radiation carries energy, angular momentum and charge. It reduces the mass of the hole. When the mass approaches the Planck mass the semi-classical calculation ceases to be reliable. The final stage of evaporation is unknown. The existence of the radiation follows from the structure of the vacuum in curved spacetime and from the presence of a horizon. It has not been observed directly. Its theoretical necessity is nevertheless required for the consistency of black-hole thermodynamics with the ordinary second law.

title: Further Aspects of the Black-Hole Information Paradox
paras: The Page curve quantifies the conflict. For a black hole that begins in a pure state the entanglement entropy of the radiated quanta must rise and then fall, returning to zero when the hole has disappeared. A strictly thermal spectrum produces a curve that rises monotonically. Any resolution that preserves unitarity must therefore introduce correlations that purify the radiation after the Page time—the moment when half the initial entropy has been emitted.

The firewall argument sharpens the same tension. If the late radiation is entangled with the early radiation (as unitarity requires) and the horizon remains a smooth vacuum (as the equivalence principle requires), then the late modes must be entangled with both the early radiation and their interior partners. Monogamy of entanglement forbids this. One of the three assumptions—unitarity, smoothness, or effective field theory outside the horizon—must fail. Complementarity attempts to evade the contradiction by denying that any single observer can access both sets of entanglements. The argument shows that the evasion is incomplete once the black hole is old.

Island calculations modify the entropy formula. After the Page time a region inside the horizon (the island) is included in the entanglement wedge of the radiation. The generalised entropy—matter entropy plus area of the quantum extremal surface—then decreases, reproducing the Page curve. The result is obtained from the semi-classical gravitational path integral in simplified models. It suggests that the interior degrees of freedom are not independent of the exterior radiation at late times. Whether the same mechanism operates for an evaporating black hole in four-dimensional asymptotically flat space remains unproven. The calculations nevertheless supply the first concrete realisation of a turning Page curve within a gravitational framework.

title: Derivation and Thermodynamics of Hawking Radiation
paras: Hawking radiation follows from the mismatch between the vacuum defined at past null infinity and the vacuum defined at future null infinity when a horizon is present. Modes that cross the horizon during collapse become entangled. Tracing over the interior partner leaves the exterior mode in a thermal state. The temperature measured at infinity is \[ T = \frac{\hbar\kappa}{2\pi k_B c}, \] where \(\kappa\) is the surface gravity. For a Schwarzschild hole \(\kappa = c^4/(4GM)\) and the familiar expression \(T = \hbar c^3/(8\pi GMk_B)\) is recovered.

The same temperature appears in the Euclidean path integral. The metric continued to imaginary time is regular at the horizon only when the period is \(2\pi/\kappa\). That period is precisely the inverse temperature of a thermal state. The agreement of the Lorentzian mode analysis and the Euclidean periodicity confirms that the radiation is thermal.

Energy conservation requires that the hole lose mass as it radiates. The luminosity scales as \(1/M^2\). The heat capacity is negative: as the hole loses mass its temperature rises and the evaporation accelerates. The process continues until the semi-classical approximation fails near the Planck mass. The thermodynamic laws of black holes—area increase, surface gravity constant on the horizon, and the first law relating mass, area and angular momentum—are satisfied by this flux. Hawking radiation is therefore required for the consistency of black-hole thermodynamics with the ordinary second law.

title: Primordial Black Holes
paras: Primordial black holes could have formed from large density perturbations in the early universe. Their masses can range from the Planck mass to many solar masses. They are constrained by the absence of evaporation signals, by microlensing, by dynamical effects and by the gravitational-wave background. In most mass windows they can constitute only a fraction of the dark matter.

The window near asteroid masses remains less constrained. A detection would constitute both a dark-matter candidate and a probe of the primordial power spectrum on small scales. No confirmed detection exists. The possibility is not excluded. It is tightly bounded.

title: The Information Paradox in AdS/CFT
paras: In AdS/CFT the formation and evaporation of a black hole is dual to the unitary evolution of a thermal state in the boundary theory. Unitarity is therefore guaranteed. The paradox becomes the question of how the bulk calculation reproduces the unitary result. The island formula and the replica wormhole provide the bulk mechanism. They modify the entropy calculation after the Page time.

The resolution is explicit in low-dimensional models and in certain supersymmetric theories. Its extension to higher-dimensional, asymptotically flat black holes is not complete. The AdS/CFT example demonstrates that a unitary resolution is possible within a consistent theory of quantum gravity. It does not yet supply the resolution for the black holes that form in our universe.

title: Firewalls
paras: The firewall argument states that unitarity, the equivalence principle and effective field theory outside the horizon cannot all be maintained for an old black hole. The monogamy of entanglement is the obstruction. One of the three assumptions must fail. A firewall is a high-energy barrier at the horizon that preserves unitarity at the cost of the equivalence principle.

The argument has not been resolved. Island calculations suggest that the interior is not independent of the exterior radiation after the Page time. The suggestion softens the conflict. It does not eliminate it for all observers. The firewall remains a possible outcome. It is not required by present calculations. The tension between unitarity and smoothness is real. Its resolution is model-dependent.

title: The Page Curve in Detail
paras: The Page curve is the entanglement entropy of the radiation as a function of time. For a unitary evaporation it rises until the Page time and then falls to zero. The rise is the accumulation of entanglement. The fall is the release of that entanglement in correlations. A thermal spectrum produces only the rise. The fall requires non-thermal correlations.

Island calculations reproduce the fall. The quantum extremal surface moves behind the horizon after the Page time. The generalised entropy decreases. The calculation is semi-classical. It captures the leading entanglement. It does not construct the microscopic operators that purify the radiation.
