Trace gases—water vapour, carbon dioxide, methane, ozone—control the radiative balance. Incoming solar radiation is partly reflected and partly absorbed. Outgoing long-wave radiation is trapped by greenhouse gases. The resulting surface temperature is approximately 33 K warmer than the effective radiating temperature.

Climate is the long-term statistics of weather. It varies on every timescale. Orbital (Milankovitch) cycles modulate the seasonal distribution of sunlight and pace the Pleistocene ice ages. Volcanic aerosols cool the surface for a few years. Changes in greenhouse-gas concentrations alter the energy budget for decades to millennia. The present rise in carbon dioxide is produced by fossil-fuel combustion and land-use change. It is occurring at a rate unprecedented in the ice-core record.

Feedbacks amplify or damp the response. Water vapour and snow–ice albedo are positive. Clouds and the carbon cycle contain both positive and negative terms. The equilibrium climate sensitivity to a doubling of carbon dioxide is estimated between 2 K and 5 K. The atmosphere and ocean together redistribute heat. The same physical principles govern the climates of other planets that possess atmospheres.

title: Planetary Atmospheres
paras: A planetary atmosphere is a gaseous envelope retained by gravity. Retention depends on the planet’s mass, radius and temperature and on the mass of the gas molecules. Light gases escape more readily. Earth retains nitrogen and oxygen but has lost most of its primordial hydrogen and helium. The giant planets retain hydrogen and helium because of their deeper gravitational wells and lower temperatures.

Composition is set by formation and by subsequent processing. Primary atmospheres are captured from the nebula. Secondary atmospheres are released by outgassing and by impacts. Photochemistry, condensation and escape then modify the mixture. Earth’s oxygen is almost entirely biological. Venus and Mars have carbon-dioxide atmospheres produced by outgassing and by the failure to sequester carbon in surface reservoirs.

Circulation is driven by differential heating. Hadley cells, jets and vortices redistribute heat. The Coriolis force organises the flow into bands on rapidly rotating planets. Greenhouse gases raise the surface temperature above the effective radiating temperature. The same radiative and dynamical principles operate on every planet that possesses an atmosphere. The outcomes differ because mass, rotation rate, distance from the star and composition differ.

title: Exoplanet Detection, Demographics and Atmospheres
paras: The radial-velocity method measures the star’s reflex motion. Precision of 1 m s\(^{-1}\) detects Jupiter-mass planets at a few astronomical units and super-Earths on close orbits. The transit method measures the periodic dimming when a planet crosses the stellar disk. The depth gives the planet-to-star radius ratio. Combined with a mass from radial velocity or from transit-timing variations, the bulk density follows.

Occurrence studies show that planets are abundant. The average number of planets per star is of order unity. Super-Earths and mini-Neptunes are the most common size class. A radius gap near 1.5–2 Earth radii separates predominantly rocky planets from those that retained substantial envelopes. Hot Jupiters exist but are rare. Rocky planets inside the habitable zones of their stars occur at rates of tens of percent around Sun-like and smaller stars.

Transmission spectroscopy during transit reveals atmospheric composition. Starlight filtered through the planetary limb carries absorption features of atoms and molecules. Water, sodium, potassium, carbon monoxide and methane have been detected. Clouds and hazes mute features on many worlds. Emission spectroscopy and phase curves measure dayside temperatures and heat redistribution. The data demonstrate that exoplanet atmospheres span a wide range of metallicities, temperature structures and aerosol properties. Biosignature searches are limited by stellar activity, cloud cover and the present precision of the observations.

title: The Great Oxidation Event
paras: The Great Oxidation Event was the first sustained rise of free oxygen in Earth’s atmosphere, occurring between approximately 2.4 and 2.1 billion years ago. Before the event the atmosphere and oceans were anoxic. Oxygen produced by cyanobacteria was consumed by reduced volcanic gases and by ferrous iron dissolved in seawater. When those sinks became saturated, oxygen accumulated.

The transition is recorded in the rock record. Detrital pyrite and uraninite, stable only under low oxygen, disappear. Red beds containing oxidised iron appear. Major banded-iron formation ceases. A pronounced positive carbon-isotope excursion indicates increased burial of organic carbon. Atmospheric oxygen rose from negligible levels to a few percent of the present concentration. The rise was permanent, although later fluctuations occurred.

The oxygenation transformed surface chemistry. It enabled aerobic respiration and thereby the higher energy yields required by large, active organisms. It also oxidised atmospheric methane, a potent greenhouse gas, and is implicated in the Huronian glaciation that followed. The event marks the point at which biological oxygen production permanently altered the planetary environment. All subsequent aerobic life depends on it.

title: The Snowball Earth Hypothesis
paras: The Snowball Earth hypothesis proposes that the planet was repeatedly covered by ice from pole to equator during the Neoproterozoic, roughly 720–635 million years ago. Two main glacial intervals—the Sturtian and the Marinoan—are recognised. Geological evidence includes glacial deposits at low palaeolatitudes, banded-iron formations that reappear after a billion-year absence, and cap carbonates that overlie the glacial strata, indicating rapid warming and high atmospheric carbon dioxide.

The proposed trigger is a runaway ice-albedo feedback. Once ice sheets reach a critical latitude, their reflectivity cools the planet further, driving the ice to the equator. Escape from the snowball state requires the accumulation of volcanic carbon dioxide to levels hundreds of times the present concentration. The resulting greenhouse warming melts the ice in a geologically short interval. The cap carbonates are the predicted chemical consequence of that deglaciation.

The hypothesis accounts for the unusual association of glacial deposits with indicators of low latitude and for the extreme carbon-isotope excursions of the Neoproterozoic. Alternative models invoke less complete ice cover—“slushball” states—with open equatorial oceans. Both versions remain under discussion. The episodes coincide with major changes in the carbon cycle and precede the appearance of the first large, complex organisms. Whether the glaciations directly facilitated that appearance is unresolved. The geological evidence for widespread, low-latitude ice is robust.

title: Climate Science
paras: Climate science is the study of the long-term statistics of the atmosphere, ocean, cryosphere and land surface, and of the forcings that change those statistics. The energy budget is central. Incoming solar radiation is balanced by reflected short-wave radiation and by outgoing long-wave radiation. Greenhouse gases alter the balance by absorbing and re-emitting infrared radiation.

Observational records include surface temperature series, satellite radiances, ocean heat content, ice-sheet mass balance and paleoclimate proxies. The instrumental record shows a global surface warming of approximately 1.1 °C since the late nineteenth century. The warming is larger over land than over ocean and larger in the Arctic than in the tropics. Attribution studies using climate models and observations assign the majority of the warming since 1950 to the increase in greenhouse gases from fossil-fuel combustion and land-use change.

Models solve the fluid equations on a rotating sphere together with radiation, convection and cloud parameterisations. They reproduce the observed warming when historical forcings are imposed and project further warming under continued emissions. Equilibrium climate sensitivity to a doubling of CO₂ lies between 2 °C and 5 °C. Regional changes in precipitation, extremes and sea level follow. The physical basis is established. The remaining uncertainties are quantitative and concern the magnitude and regional distribution of future change.

title: Further Aspects of Climate Science
paras: Paleoclimate records extend the instrumental series. Ice cores provide continuous archives of temperature, greenhouse-gas concentrations and dust for the past 800 000 years. Ocean sediments and corals supply longer but less finely resolved records. These proxies show that CO₂ and temperature have varied together through the glacial cycles, with CO₂ lagging the initial orbital trigger and then amplifying it.

The carbon-cycle feedbacks are central. Warmer oceans hold less dissolved CO₂. Thawing permafrost and increased respiration release additional carbon. These positive feedbacks are already observable. Negative feedbacks—increased weathering, possible fertilisation of marine productivity—operate on longer timescales. The net effect on century scales is positive.

Sea-level rise has two components: thermal expansion of seawater and the addition of water from melting glaciers and ice sheets. Both are under way. The Greenland and Antarctic ice sheets contain enough ice to raise sea level by approximately 7 m and 58 m respectively if fully melted. Current mass-loss rates are accelerating. The committed rise from past emissions is already tens of centimetres. Future rise depends on emissions and on the still-uncertain dynamics of ice-sheet collapse.

title: Exoplanet Atmospheres
paras: Transmission spectroscopy measures the wavelength-dependent radius of a transiting planet. Absorption features reveal atoms and molecules. Water, sodium, potassium, carbon monoxide and methane have been detected. Clouds and hazes mute the features on many worlds. Emission spectroscopy measures the dayside temperature structure. Phase curves measure the longitudinal heat transport.

The data show a wide range of metallicities, carbon-to-oxygen ratios and thermal profiles. Hot Jupiters exhibit temperature inversions when irradiated strongly enough to maintain optical absorbers. Smaller planets show diverse compositions. The observations are limited by stellar activity and by the precision of present instruments. They already demonstrate that exoplanet atmospheres are not scaled versions of Solar-System atmospheres. They are a new regime.

title: The Carbon-Silicate Cycle
paras: The carbon-silicate cycle is the long-term regulator of Earth’s climate. Volcanism releases CO₂. Weathering of silicate rocks consumes it. The weathering rate increases with temperature and with runoff. The feedback is negative. It stabilises the climate on million-year timescales. Burial of carbonate and organic carbon removes carbon from the surface reservoirs. Subduction returns it to the mantle.

The cycle has operated for billions of years. It kept the surface temperature within the range that permits liquid water. Perturbations—large igneous provinces, changes in continental configuration—produce excursions. The excursions are temporary. The cycle restores balance. It is the principal reason Earth’s climate has remained habitable despite a brightening Sun and varying volcanic input.

title: Snowball Earth Events
paras: Two major Snowball Earth glaciations occurred in the Neoproterozoic. Ice reached low latitudes. Escape required the accumulation of volcanic CO₂ to levels hundreds of times the present concentration. The subsequent deglaciation was rapid. Cap carbonates record the event. The glaciations coincide with major changes in the carbon cycle and precede the appearance of large complex organisms.

Whether the ice cover was complete or whether equatorial oceans remained open is debated. Both versions are consistent with the geological evidence. The events demonstrate that the climate system can enter and exit extreme states. They also demonstrate that the carbon-silicate cycle can restore habitable conditions even after global glaciation. The recovery is recorded in the rocks.

title: Human Evolution
paras: Human evolution is the phylogenetic history of the hominin lineage after its divergence from the chimpanzee lineage, approximately 6–7 million years ago. Early hominins were bipedal and small-brained. The genus Homo appears around 2.8 million years ago. Brain size increases thereafter. Stone tools appear by 3.3 million years ago. The Acheulean industry is associated with Homo erectus. Control of fire is documented by 1 million years ago.

Homo sapiens emerges in Africa around 300 000 years ago. Anatomically modern humans disperse out of Africa after 60 000 years ago. They interbreed with Neanderthals and Denisovans. Those archaic populations disappear. Genetic data show that non-African populations carry 1–2 percent Neanderthal ancestry. Some Oceanian populations carry additional Denisovan ancestry.

Cultural evolution accelerates. Symbolic behaviour, complex tools and, later, agriculture and writing appear. Biological evolution continues but is now accompanied by rapid cultural and technological change. The fossil, archaeological and genetic records converge on an African origin of Homo sapiens and on subsequent global dispersal with limited archaic admixture.

title: Australopithecus and Early Hominins
paras: The hominin lineage diverged from the chimpanzee lineage between 7 and 6 million years ago. The earliest well-sampled genus is Australopithecus, appearing around 4.2 million years ago. Australopithecus afarensis, known from East Africa, was bipedal yet retained arboreal adaptations. Brain size was only slightly larger than that of chimpanzees. Sexual dimorphism was pronounced.

Other species—Australopithecus africanus in South Africa, Australopithecus sediba, and the robust australopiths (Paranthropus)—show dietary and locomotor variation. Stone-tool use is documented by 3.3 million years ago, before the appearance of Homo. The australopiths demonstrate that bipedalism preceded significant brain enlargement. They occupy the morphological and temporal interval between earlier, poorly known hominins and the genus Homo. Their extinction coincides with the rise of early Homo and with environmental shifts toward more open habitats.

title: Homo erectus and the First Dispersals
paras: Homo erectus appears in Africa around 1.9 million years ago. Brain size is substantially larger than in australopiths. Body proportions approach those of modern humans. The Acheulean stone-tool industry, characterised by hand-axes, is associated with the species. Control of fire is securely documented by 1 million years ago and may be older.

Homo erectus was the first hominin to leave Africa. Fossils and tools in Georgia, China and Indonesia date to between 1.8 and 1.6 million years ago. The dispersals demonstrate that a hominin with a larger brain, more efficient locomotion and improved technology could occupy a wide range of environments. Regional populations persisted for more than a million years. The species is the probable ancestor of both later African Homo and of the archaic Eurasian lineages that include Neanderthals and Denisovans.

title: Neanderthals and Denisovans
paras: Neanderthals occupied Europe and western Asia from approximately 400 000 to 40 000 years ago. They possessed large brains, robust skeletons and a Mousterian tool culture. Genetic data show that they interbred with anatomically modern humans. Non-African populations today carry 1–2 percent Neanderthal ancestry. The introgressed alleles affect skin, hair and immune function.

Denisovans are known primarily from DNA recovered from fragmentary remains in Siberia and from sediments. They contributed ancestry to modern Oceanian and some Asian populations. Both Neanderthals and Denisovans are sister groups to Homo sapiens within the genus Homo. Their extinction coincides with the arrival of modern humans in their respective ranges. The genetic legacy demonstrates that the replacement was not complete. Archaic admixture is a documented feature of recent human evolution.

title: Homo naledi
paras: Homo naledi is a hominin species known from the Rising Star cave system in South Africa. The remains of at least fifteen individuals have been recovered from the Dinaledi Chamber. The skeleton combines primitive and derived features. The shoulders, trunk and pelvis are australopith-like. The hands, feet and dentition are closer to later Homo. Brain volume is small, approximately 500 cm\(^3\).

Dating of the fossils yields an age between 335 000 and 236 000 years ago. The species therefore coexisted with early Homo sapiens in Africa. The location of the remains deep inside a cave system that lacks evidence of occupation has prompted the hypothesis that the bodies were deliberately placed there. Alternative explanations—natural trapping or water transport—have not been excluded. No associated stone tools or other cultural remains have been found in the chamber.

Homo naledi demonstrates that morphological diversity within Homo persisted into the later Middle Pleistocene. A small-brained species with a mosaic of primitive and derived traits lived alongside larger-brained hominins. Its phylogenetic position remains unresolved. It may represent a surviving lineage of early Homo or a convergent form. The fossils enlarge the known range of hominin variation in the period immediately preceding the appearance of anatomically modern humans.

title: Homo habilis
paras: Homo habilis is the earliest widely recognised species of the genus Homo. Fossils from East Africa date between approximately 2.4 and 1.4 million years ago. Brain volume averages about 600 cm\(^3\), larger than australopiths yet smaller than later Homo. The face is less projecting. The hands show adaptations for precision gripping.

The species is associated with the Oldowan stone-tool industry—simple flakes and cores. Whether habilis itself made the tools is inferred from chronological and spatial coincidence. Body size remained small. Locomotion was fully bipedal. The taxonomic boundaries are debated. Some specimens may belong to Australopithecus or to a separate early Homo species. Regardless of the precise allocation, the fossils document the appearance of larger brains and systematic tool use in the hominin lineage by 2.4 million years ago.

title: Homo heidelbergensis
paras: Homo heidelbergensis is a Middle Pleistocene species known from Africa and Europe, dated between roughly 700 000 and 200 000 years ago. Brain size overlaps the modern human range, averaging 1 200 cm\(^3\). The species is associated with the later Acheulean industry and with the earliest evidence of constructed shelters and of hafted spears.

African populations of heidelbergensis are regarded by many researchers as the ancestors of Homo sapiens. European populations are regarded as the ancestors of Neanderthals. The species therefore occupies the last common ancestral position before the sapiens–Neanderthal divergence. Regional variation is considerable. Some authors prefer to split the sample into additional taxa. The fossils nevertheless document a hominin with a large brain, advanced tools and a wide geographic range in the Middle Pleistocene.

title: Homo floresiensis
paras: Homo floresiensis is a small-bodied hominin known from the island of Flores, Indonesia. The type specimen dates to approximately 60 000 years ago. Additional remains extend the temporal range. Adult stature was about 1.1 m. Brain volume was approximately 400 cm\(^3\). Stone tools are associated with the remains.

The diminutive size has been interpreted as island dwarfism acting on an earlier Homo erectus population, or as the persistence of an even earlier, small-bodied lineage. Pathological explanations for the type specimen have been excluded by the discovery of additional individuals. The species demonstrates that hominins reached Wallacea and that isolated populations could evolve extreme body-size reduction. Its survival until at least 50 000 years ago means it overlapped in time with modern humans in the broader region. The phylogenetic placement remains uncertain.

title: Further Detail on Human Evolution
paras: The hominin fossil record now includes more than twenty named species. The sequence is not a single line. Multiple species coexisted for long intervals. Australopithecus and early Homo overlapped. Homo erectus persisted in Asia while other lineages evolved in Africa. Neanderthals, Denisovans and Homo sapiens overlapped in time and interbred.

Genetic data calibrate the divergences. The human–chimpanzee split is dated to 7–6 million years ago. The sapiens–Neanderthal split is dated to approximately 600 000 years ago. Introgression from Neanderthals into non-African modern humans occurred after 60 000 years ago. Denisovan introgression is highest in Oceanian populations. The admixture events are detected by the excess sharing of derived alleles and by the length distribution of introgressed haplotypes.

Cultural evidence appears early. Stone tools at 3.3 million years ago, cut-marked bones, ochre use by 300 000 years ago, and symbolic artefacts after 100 000 years ago. The acceleration of cultural change after 50 000 years ago coincides with the global dispersal of Homo sapiens. Biological and cultural evolution have proceeded together since the origin of the genus. The genetic and fossil records are mutually consistent on the broad outline.

title: Further Aspects of Neanderthals and Denisovans
paras: Neanderthal genomes recovered from bones and from cave sediments show that the population was small and structured. Genetic diversity was lower than in modern humans. The low diversity is consistent with repeated bottlenecks. Adaptive alleles introgressed into modern humans include variants that affect skin and hair pigmentation and immune response. Some of the introgressed haplotypes are associated with increased risk of certain diseases. The net effect of the admixture was not uniformly beneficial.

Denisovan ancestry is highest in populations of New Guinea and Australia, reaching 4–6 percent. The introgressed segments include alleles that improve adaptation to high altitude in Tibetans. The source population of the Denisovan contribution appears to have been diverse. At least two distinct Denisovan lineages contributed. The genetic evidence therefore reveals a more complex history of archaic admixture than the fossil record alone had indicated.

title: Further Aspects of Homo heidelbergensis
paras: Homo heidelbergensis is defined morphologically by a combination of archaic and derived traits. Brain size overlaps the modern range. The brow ridge is prominent. The species is associated with the later Acheulean and with the earliest wooden spears, found at Schöningen and dated to approximately 300 000 years ago. The spears demonstrate planned hunting of large game.

African specimens are often regarded as the direct ancestors of Homo sapiens. European specimens are regarded as the ancestors of Neanderthals. The geographic split is supported by both morphology and by the genetic divergence date of approximately 600 000 years ago. Some researchers prefer to assign the African and European samples to separate species. The fossils nevertheless document a large-brained, wide-ranging hominin that occupied the ancestral position before the sapiens–Neanderthal split.

title: Further Aspects of Australopithecus
paras: Australopithecus afarensis is known from dozens of individuals, including the partial skeleton Lucy. The pelvis and knee are adapted for bipedalism. The arms and curved fingers retain arboreal capability. Sexual dimorphism is high. Brain size is 380–430 cm\(^3\). Footprints at Laetoli, dated to 3.6 million years ago, confirm bipedal gait with a human-like stride.

Other species show dietary specialisation. Paranthropus developed massive jaws and molars for processing tough vegetation. Australopithecus sediba combines australopith and Homo-like features and has been proposed as a close relative of early Homo. The genus as a whole demonstrates that bipedalism and modest brain enlargement preceded the appearance of the genus Homo. The later extinction of the australopiths coincides with the expansion of early Homo and with increasing environmental variability.

title: Further Aspects of Homo floresiensis
paras: Homo floresiensis persisted on Flores until at least 50 000 years ago. Stone tools associated with the species are found in deposits that span hundreds of thousands of years. The tools are simple yet consistent. They indicate a stable technological tradition maintained by a small-bodied population.

The island setting supplies the selective context for dwarfism. Limited resources and the absence of large predators favour reduced body size in large mammals. The same process is documented in other island lineages. Whether floresiensis descended from Homo erectus or from an earlier, smaller-bodied migrant remains unresolved. The brain size of approximately 400 cm\(^3\) is smaller than that of any other Homo species except the earliest. The combination of small brain, small body and persistent tool use shows that technological behaviour is not strictly proportional to absolute brain volume.

title: Further Aspects of Homo habilis
paras: Homo habilis is associated with the Oldowan industry at multiple East African sites. The tools consist of flakes struck from cores. Use-wear studies show that the flakes were used to cut meat and plant material. The association is chronological and spatial. Direct evidence that habilis itself manufactured the tools is inferential.

Body size estimates range from 30 to 50 kg. Limb proportions are more human-like than those of australopiths, yet the arms remain relatively long. Brain size varies from 500 to 700 cm\(^3\). The variation has led some workers to split the sample into more than one species. Whether the split is justified or whether the sample represents a single variable species remains debated. The fossils document the earliest widely accepted members of the genus Homo and the first systematic production of stone tools.
